Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

suffer verb

undergo something bad

also endure, put up with, go through, suffer a wrong, suffer a defeat, suffering, put up with someone, bear with, hold out, last (go on)

classical

Liv. 2.12.9: et facere et patī fortia Rōmānum est
Phaedr. 3.7.11: nunc patior nivēs
Traupman 387

patior, patī, passus sum

verb, third conjugation (-ior), deponent

suffer, undergo, bear

Also “allow”: patī ab igne ignem capere, to let someone light a fire from yours (Cic. Off. 1.52).

Other words

  • perferō, perferre, pertulī, perlātum — bear to the end, endure

    verb · also used · classical · Catull. 8.11: sed obstinātā mente perfer, obdūrā

  • accipiō, accipere, accēpī, acceptum — suffer, receive (a wrong, a defeat, a loss)

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 5.56: accipere quam facere praestat injūriam; Traupman 186: clādem accipere, to suffer a defeat

    Of what one is dealt: injūriam, clādem accipere. To suffer a loss: damnum facere (see loss).

  • ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum — bear, put up with

    verb · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 138: quod fors feret, ferēmus aequō animō; Traupman 387

  • perpetior, perpetī, perpessus sum — put up with, bear patiently, endure to the end

    verb, third conjugation (-iō), deponent, transitive · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.77: facile omnēs perpetior ac perferō (Lewis & Short); Traupman 106: put up with s.o., aliquem perpetior

  • dūrō, dūrāre, dūrāvī, dūrātum — hold out, endure, last

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Am. 3.2.1: dūrāre nequeō in aedibus (Lewis & Short); Traupman 328; Traupman 337

  • perdūrō, perdūrāre, perdūrāvī, perdūrātum — last, hold out to the end

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Traupman 337

    (poetic and post-Augustan (Lewis & Short))

Examples

  • et facere et patī fortia Rōmānum est

    to act bravely and to suffer bravely is the Roman wayLiv. 2.12.9

  • nunc patior nivēs imbrēsque in silvīs asperam vītam trahēns

    as it is, I put up with snow and rain in the woods, dragging out a hard lifePhaedr. 3.7.11–12

  • accipere quam facere praestat injūriam

    it is better to suffer a wrong than to do oneCic. Tusc. 5.56

  • quod acerbum fuit ferre, tulisse jūcundum est

    what was hard to bear is pleasant to have borneSen. Ep. 78.14

See also suffer, loss, patient.
